Q: com.pairip.licensecheck.LicenseClient calls System.exit() — app process terminated with no crash record (REASON_EXIT_SELF) A: 
It is Google Play's **automatic protection** (`com.pairip.licensecheck`), and the reason no scan of your own build finds it is that **it is not in the artifact you upload**. Play injects it into your app after upload, at distribution time.

That is the whole trap: your source, your AAB and your dex are all clean, because you are inspecting the artifact from *before* Play modified it.

## How to confirm

Play Console → Bundle Explorer → Downloads → **"Signed, universal APK"**. Do not use "Original file" , that is your own build output and will not contain it. Then search it for `com.pairip`.

Compare against a build made with the setting off, as a control. A zero on its own tells you nothing , a wrong path, a stale artifact and a true negative all look identical.

Mine, from byte-identical source:

    protection on:   3,283,142 bytes, com.pairip present
    protection off:  3,233,990 bytes, com.pairip absent

A difference of exactly 49,152 bytes.

## What it does

Captured with a JVM shutdown hook. The exiting thread parks in `Thread.join` inside `Runtime.exit` while hooks run, so the caller's frame is still live:

    com.pairip.licensecheck.LicenseClient$1.run(LicenseClient.java:82)
    com.pairip.licensecheck.LicenseClient.createCloseAppIntentOrExitIfAppInBackground(LicenseClient.java:681)
    com.pairip.licensecheck.LicenseClient.startErrorDialogActivity(LicenseClient.java:672)
    com.pairip.licensecheck.LicenseClient.lambda$handleError$0(LicenseClient.java:659)
    java.lang.System.exit(System.java:1488)
    java.lang.Runtime.exit(Runtime.java:159)

The method name states the branch: show an error dialog if the app is in the **foreground**, terminate the process if it is in the **background**.

Google's Play Console support assistant describes it the same way: *"If the runtime check fails or cannot display an error dialog, it stops your app from running by terminating the process."*

So a background process,  a bound service, a headless component, anything with no Activity on screen, cannot take the dialog branch, and is terminated instead.

There is a second, foreground form of the same error path, where `startErrorDialogActivity` calls `startActivity`, blocks on a binder transaction and produces an ANR instead. See [flutter/flutter#175068](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/175068) for a capture of that variant.

## Why it is nearly undetectable

The termination produces **no crash record**. It surfaces only as `REASON_EXIT_SELF` in `ApplicationExitInfo`, which is indistinguishable from your own app calling `exit()`, and generates nothing in Android Vitals or Crashlytics.

## How to capture it yourself

    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread {
        // Thread.getAllStackTraces() here — the exiting thread is still
        // parked in Thread.join inside Runtime.exit, so its stack is live
    })

Write the result to app-private storage. The dying process cannot upload it, so have the *next* process read that file at startup and carry it out.

## Mitigation

Play Console → App integrity → Protected with Play → **Automatic protection**, off. The setting is applied when Play processes an upload, so it is baked into whichever artifact you upload next — flip it, then upload.

## Scope

This is not a claim that the check is wrong to fail. On my devices the reason it fails is still unidentified. It is a note that a failed check terminates a licensed, Play-installed app's background process silently, and that no developer-side inspection of your own artifact can find the code responsible.

Reported to Google via Play Console → Help → App integrity → Automatic protection, 31 August 2026.

Q: Interactive shell using Docker Compose A:

Option 1: If your container's image already has CMD set to a shell (like alpine does), then:

docker-compose run myapp

where myapp is the service name in your compose.yml, should do the deal. It respects all your compose configuration, including depends_on and shared volumes and networks. But unlike up, it attaches a tty to the container specified.

Option 2: If your container's image has CMD set to something else, then:

docker-compose run myapp sh

should do the deal. It overrides the value of CMD with whatever you specify as the last argument, here sh.

Option 3: If however, your container's image has an ENTRYPOINT set, then option 2 will append sh as an argument to the end of it. That's likely not what you want, so use this instead:

docker-compose run --entrypoint sh myapp

Note there's no command argument at the end. This overrides the entrypoint of the image with sh.

There is some confusion with up/run, but docker-compose run docs have great explanation: https://docs.docker.com/compose/reference/run

Q: SGEN : error : Mixed mode assembly A:

I found two solutions worked for this problem. One way was to add the sgen.exe.config file as mentioned in the other answers. I use Process Monitor from Sysinternals to find the exact location of sgen.exe.config. Make a filter of "Path contains sgen.exe.config" and then rebuild your project to see which config file sgen.exe is reading from.

The other solution was to change ToolPath="$(SGenToolPath)", which is what I had, to ToolPath="$(TargetFrameworkSDKToolsDirectory)" in the <SGen ... /> task in the .csproj file.

Q: How do I tell PyLint "it's a variable, not a constant" to stop message C0103? A:

Five answers for disabling the check, one for refactoring. Here's one for How do I tell PyLint "it's a variable, not a constant":

At least as far back as Pylint 2.17.7, the criteria for a global (module-level) constant is:

any variable defined at module level that is not bound to a class object.

So, somewhat counter-intuitively, one way to convince PyLint it really is a variable is to initialise it to an object, instead of a literal.

For example:

logger = "MyLogger"
run_thread = None
last_run_time = 0

All trigger invalid-name since they look to PyLint like constants.

However,

logger = logging.getLogger("MyLogger")
run_thread = threading.Thread(target=lambda: None)
last_run_time = time.time() - 999

All pass as variables!

There's an extra complication (or bonus, depending on your experience) in PyLint 4. Now globals also get classified as variables if they "are reassigned". However, the logic to determine "reassigned" is subtle. The reassignment needs to be sometimes. Using exclusive assignment doesn't do it. See the link for examples, and this long thread for a discussion. FWIW, I haven't found it reliable in practice.
